VOI. 41 supp. SCIENCE IN CHINA (Series D) December 1998 Paleomagnetic result of the Lower-Cretaceous from Luanping basin, Hebei Province and its tectonic implications * SUN Zhiming (M\%Pfl), YANG Zhenyu (@jEZ), MA Xinghua (qEq) and ZHAO Yue ( & &!4) (Institute of Geomechanics, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing 100081, China) Received September 16, 1998 Abstract A paleomagnetic study of about 95 samples from 16 sites sampled in the Early Cretaceous in Luanping basin in Hebei Province was reported. Stepwise thermal demagnetization was used to isolate magnetic components. Most samples have a characteristic direction with a high temperature component above 50093 . The tectonic-corrected data are D = 347.8'. I = 50.4'. ass = 7. lo, and the corresponding pole position is at 76. ION, 346.3'E, with dp = 6.4". dm = 3.8', paleolatitude A = 31.1°N. This result indicates a counterclockwise post-Cretaceous rotation of 30.7" + 9.8" with respect to the stable Ordos basin in the west of North China Block, and a non-significant northward mo- tion. This rotation could be related to local fault action or structural detachment, or regional NNW-NWWward motion and collision of Kula-Pacific plate with eastern China since the Early Cret

This rotation could be related to local fault action or structural detachment, or regional NNW-NWWward motion and collision of Kula-Pacific plate with eastern China since the Early Cretaceous. Keywords: Luanping basin, Early Cretaceous, counterclockwise rotation, Kula-Pacific plate. Since the 1980s, a large number of paleomagnetic studies have been carried out in the Ordos basin in the west of North China Block (NCB)['-~]. A number of reliable Jurassic-Cretaceous pa- leomagnetic data have been obtained to establish the apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the whole NCB, and to provide important fundamental information for studying its structural evolu- tion. A lot of geological studies have shown the distinct tectonic differential movement between the eastern and western part of NCB since the Mesozoic. The western part of NCB is character- ized by large Jurassic-Cretaceous fault basin, while the eastern part is characterized by small Mid- dle Jurassic-Cretaceous fault basin, large scale magmatic explosion and intrusion, and severe struc- tural activity. So, paleomagnetic studies may contribute to a better understanding of the Mesozoic evolution of NCB by correlating the Jurassic-Cretaceous paleomagnetic data with that from other tectonic units. A c

nding of the Mesozoic evolution of NCB by correlating the Jurassic-Cretaceous paleomagnetic data with that from other tectonic units. A considerable amount of paleomagnetic studies have been carried out in the Juras- sic-Cretaceous sediments in the eastern part of NCB. It is difficult to interpret the paleomagnetic data because of the complex structure, multi-periodic volcanic activity and widespread remagneti- zation related to the Yanshannian orogeny in this region. In this paper we report the paleomagnet- ic result obtained from lower Cretaceous sediments in Luanping basin, and discuss its tectonic im- plications by comparison with paleomagnetic results from adjacent blocks. 1 Sampling and paleomagnetic measurements The Luanping basin is one of the regions in NCB in which the late Jurassic-early Cretaceous volcanic sediments are well developed. region The Proterozoic cover succession in the NCB has been divided into the Changchengian (ca. 1 800ü1 400 Ma), the Jixianian (ca. 1 400 ü1 000 Ma), the Qingbaikouan (ca. 1 000ü800 Ma) 234 SCIENCE IN CHINA (Series D) V ol. 43 and the Sinian (ca. 800 ü545 Ma) systems. The type section of the first three systems is in Jixian. There is a sedimentation hiatus through the Sinian to the earliest Cambrian in Jixian, but strata of that age interval are well develop ed in Fuzhou, Xu-H uai and along the southern margin of the craton. We have selected the Lusha n region in western Henan Province for this study (fig.1) be- cause (1) there is a fairly complete succe ssion from the late Mesoproterozoic to the Lower Cam- brian, and (2) the structure there is simple. The type section of the first three systems is in Jixian. There is a sedimentation hiatus through the Sinian to the earliest Cambrian in Jixian, but strata of that age interval are well develop ed in Fuzhou, Xu-H uai and along the southern margin of the craton. We have selected the Lusha n region in western Henan Province for this study (fig.1) be- cause (1) there is a fairly complete succe ssion from the late Mesoproterozoic to the Lower Cam- brian, and (2) the structure there is simple. The Peri Rhyolite has been correlated with the Eastons Arm Rhyolite of the southern Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11). The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006 2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag- netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified (Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’). This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite, which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with the Peri Rhyolite. In contrast, Opdyke et al. (2000), follow- ing earlier workers (Hocking 1973; Stroud 1990b), regarded this Boomi Creek succession as a minor thrust sliver belonging to the Caroda Formation. The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000) near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006 2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag- netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified (Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’). This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite, which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with the Peri Rhyolite. In contrast, Opdyke et al. (2000), follow- ing earlier workers (Hocking 1973; Stroud 1990b), regarded this Boomi Creek succession as a minor thrust sliver belonging to the Caroda Formation. The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000) near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). A SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 310.6/H110064.0 Ma indicates a late Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6). The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. Sampling of the middle Visean to Westphalian– Stephanian volcanic-rich succession of the Rocky Creek Block (64 sites, 734 samples) has been carried out in three phases. Reconnaissance sampling (17 sites, 171 samples) was carried out in 1987. Preliminary palaeomagnetic results from this collection were listed in Klootwijk (1996a) and their implications were discussed in an initial syn- thesis of the Carboniferous palaeomagnetism of the Tamworth Belt (Klootwijk 1996b). Extensive follow-up sampling (41 sites, 492 samples) was carried out in 1995 for comprehensive stratigraphic coverage of the successions and for fold tests. Sampling was complemented in 1999 with a small collection (6 sites, 71 samples) to strengthen the palaeomagnetic record of the Clifden Formation. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: . Well-defined triaxial ellipsoids are also prominent, but various sites do not have a clear magnetic fabric pattern. The potential of magnetic fabric analysis for determin- ation of transport directions in ignimbrites and trans- ported air-fall tuffs has been well established from pioneering studies on felsic volcanic rocks, mainly Cenozoic, in southwestern North America (MacDonald & Palmer 1990; Palmer et al. 1991). Such studies have shown that the K min axis of the AMS ellipsoid generally represents the pole to the foliation or flow-banding plane, that the K max axis parallels the flow- or transport-axis, and that imbrication of coarser components within the volcanic rocks can be used as an indication of transport direction with the source expected in the downdip direction of imbrication. The method can only be applied reliably if it can be established that the AMS ellipsoids reflect primary depositional patterns and not tectonic deformation. The in situ K max axes of the volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks of the Rocky Creek Block show an overall north– south alignment (Figure 10b). The regional tectonic grain is also north–south (Figures 3, 4) and a tectonic origin of the AMS pattern might, therefore, be surmised at first glance. INTERPRETATION Overprint magnetisations: post-folding MIDDLE–LATE CENOZOIC OVERPRINTS A magnetically soft overprint of exclusively normal polarity and with in situ directions close to the present local field direction is consistently present throughout the sites (Figure 12a, b). This component is unblocked at temperatures up to 300°C and in alternating fields up to 30 mT . Its mean direction is indistinguishable from a present field component in the southward adjacent Werrie Block. Both are similar to an overprint observed on the south coast of New South Wales and interpreted as Early Miocene in age (Nott et al. 1991). This set of over- prints may be indicative of a regional mid-Tertiary weathering event, although the overprints’ exclusive normal polarity and closeness to the present local field direction alternatively may point to a recent viscous origin. SAMPLING Sampling strategy An initial pilot study of the Tamworth Belt succession, on the Lower Carboniferous volcano-sedimentary succession of the Upper Rouchel region, demonstrated that ignimbritic volcanics can retain their primary magnetisation, despite conditions leading to pervasive overprinting of inter- calated volcaniclastic rocks. These may have induced magnetic overprints on the studied successions of the Rocky Creek Block, requir- ing careful analysis and interpretation of the palaeo- magnetic data in order to separate and identify primary and overprint components, and perhaps incompletely cleaned pseudo-components. Sampling of the middle Visean to Westphalian– Stephanian volcanic-rich succession of the Rocky Creek Block (64 sites, 734 samples) has been carried out in three phases. Reconnaissance sampling (17 sites, 171 samples) was carried out in 1987. Preliminary palaeomagnetic results from this collection were listed in Klootwijk (1996a) and their implications were discussed in an initial syn- thesis of the Carboniferous palaeomagnetism of the Tamworth Belt (Klootwijk 1996b). Extensive follow-up sampling (41 sites, 492 samples) was carried out in 1995 for comprehensive stratigraphic coverage of the successions and for fold tests. Sampling was complemented in 1999 with a small collection (6 sites, 71 samples) to strengthen the palaeomagnetic record of the Clifden Formation. This sampling also addressed the stratigraphic position of the Boomi Rhyolite – Kooringal Dacite succession, generally considered part of the Caroda Formation, but interpreted herein as part of the Clifden Formation. Samples were collected with a portable drill, an adapted STIHL auger , using a water jacket for cooling and stainless steel barrels for reduced magnetic contamination. MAGNETIC TREATMENT, ANALYSIS AND INTERPRETATION METHODS Sample preparation All core samples were sandblasted to remove possible mag- netic contamination from the stainless-steel drill barrels, and were sliced into standard specimens, 2.54 cm diameter and 2.2 cm height. Top and bottom of the specimens were ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen per sample. Alternating-field (AF) demagnetisation was carried out on one representative specimen per site and rock magnetic studies on one other specimen per site. Palaeomagnetic treatment One specimen per sample was subjected to progressive thermal demagnetisation in 18–36 steps up to peak temper- atures of 695°C. Thermal demagnetisation was carried out in large-volume furnaces (McElhinny et al. 1971) at the centre of feedback-controlled Rubens–Helmholtz coil systems (10 coils), which reduce the ambient magnetic field to less than 5 nT over the heating–cooling cycle. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: . Well-defined triaxial ellipsoids are also prominent, but various sites do not have a clear magnetic fabric pattern. The potential of magnetic fabric analysis for determin- ation of transport directions in ignimbrites and trans- ported air-fall tuffs has been well established from pioneering studies on felsic volcanic rocks, mainly Cenozoic, in southwestern North America (MacDonald & Palmer 1990; Palmer et al. 1991). Such studies have shown that the K min axis of the AMS ellipsoid generally represents the pole to the foliation or flow-banding plane, that the K max axis parallels the flow- or transport-axis, and that imbrication of coarser components within the volcanic rocks can be used as an indication of transport direction with the source expected in the downdip direction of imbrication. The method can only be applied reliably if it can be established that the AMS ellipsoids reflect primary depositional patterns and not tectonic deformation. The in situ K max axes of the volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks of the Rocky Creek Block show an overall north– south alignment (Figure 10b). The regional tectonic grain is also north–south (Figures 3, 4) and a tectonic origin of the AMS pattern might, therefore, be surmised at first glance. Palaeomagnetic, rock magnetic and magnetic fabric results are presented for a Carboniferous (Visean to Westphalian) succession of felsic, mainly ignimbritic, volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks from the Rocky Creek Block of the northern Tamworth Belt, southern New England Orogen. Detailed thermal demagnetisation of 734 samples from 64 sites show three groups of magnetic components with low (<300°C), intermediate (300–600°C) and high (500–680°C) unblocking temperature ranges. Well-defined primary magnetisations have been determined for 28 sites with evidence of four overprint phases. The overprints arise from a mid-Tertiary weathering event (or possibly recent viscous origin), and from fluid movements associated with the Late Cretaceous opening of the Tasman Sea, thrusting during the Middle Triassic main phase of the Hunter–Bowen Orogeny, and latest Carboniferous – Early Permian formation of the Bowen–Gunnedah–Sydney Basin system. The Peri Rhyolite has been correlated with the Eastons Arm Rhyolite of the southern Rocky Creek Syncline (Opdyke et al. 2000 figures 4, 5, 11). The Eastons Arm Rhyolite (317.8 /H110062.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) and the underlying Wanganui Andesite (319.2 /H11006 2.8 Ma: Opdyke et al. 2000) are of reverse and normal mag- netic polarity , respectively , and have been identified (Opdyke et al. 2000) to constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron (or ‘Kiaman’). This pair of volcanic rocks is of great significance for global correlation and dating. It is discussed herein that the volcanic pair of Boomi Rhyolite and Kooringal Dacite, which crops out in Boomi Creek directly east of the Kathrose Fault (Figures 4, 6), likewise may constrain the lower boundary of the Permo-Carboniferous Reverse Superchron, with the Boomi Rhyolite correlatable with the Peri Rhyolite. In contrast, Opdyke et al. (2000), follow- ing earlier workers (Hocking 1973; Stroud 1990b), regarded this Boomi Creek succession as a minor thrust sliver belonging to the Caroda Formation. The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. Deformation phases The New England Orogen has a long history of tectonic activity . Up to eight tectonic phases have been identified for the period from Devonian to the Late Cretaceous opening of the Tasman Sea (Korsch & Harrington 1981; Harrington & Korsch 1985a; Veevers et al. 1994b; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Tamworth Belt has been affected strongly by four of the phases. These may have induced magnetic overprints on the studied successions of the Rocky Creek Block, requir- ing careful analysis and interpretation of the palaeo- magnetic data in order to separate and identify primary and overprint components, and perhaps incompletely cleaned pseudo-components. The oldest of these four Carboniferous tectonic phases relates to development of the erosional disconformity between the lower and upper succession. Magnetic over- prints close to the top of the eroded succession may result from chemical processes during erosion, or may be due to fluid-flow that used the erosional disconformity as a pathway . The second tectonic phase had a major effect on the shape of the New England Orogen. MAGNETIC TREATMENT, ANALYSIS AND INTERPRETATION METHODS Sample preparation All core samples were sandblasted to remove possible mag- netic contamination from the stainless-steel drill barrels, and were sliced into standard specimens, 2.54 cm diameter and 2.2 cm height. Top and bottom of the specimens were ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen per sample. Alternating-field (AF) demagnetisation was carried out on one representative specimen per site and rock magnetic studies on one other specimen per site. Palaeomagnetic treatment One specimen per sample was subjected to progressive thermal demagnetisation in 18–36 steps up to peak temper- atures of 695°C. Thermal demagnetisation was carried out in large-volume furnaces (McElhinny et al. 1971) at the centre of feedback-controlled Rubens–Helmholtz coil systems (10 coils), which reduce the ambient magnetic field to less than 5 nT over the heating–cooling cycle. The upper unit of the upper succession, the Lark Hill Formation, has been sampled along Tops Road in the northern Rocky Creek Block and along Rocky Creek in the central Rocky Creek Block (Figure 4). Prominent volcanic horizons on the Tops Road section are the brownish-green Tycannah Rhyodacite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000) near its base and the greenish-reddish Tops Ignimbrite (Johnson 1971; Opdyke et al. 2000). The Rocky Creek section is characterised by greenish, pinkish ash-rich cherty siltstone of redeposited pyroclastic origin, known as the Eulowrie Pyroclastics (Hocking 1973; Opdyke et al. 2000). A SHRIMP U–Pb zircon age of 310.6/H110064.0 Ma indicates a late Westphalian age (Figures 5, 6). The Eulowrie Pyroclastics and the underlying cherty diamictites of the Rocky Creek Conglomerate were first analysed by Irving (1966) in his pioneering palaeomagnetic study of Carboniferous volcanics of the Tamworth Belt. Widespread occurrence of magnetic overprints of Permo-Carboniferous (Schmidt 1988; Klootwijk 1996b) and Permo-Triassic age (Lackie & Schmidt 1993) throughout the Tamworth Belt succession and the Carboniferous succession of the Texas and Coffs Harbour Oroclines (Aubourg et al. 1994) has become well established. Therefore, sampling of the Rocky Creek Block concentrated on the frequent volcanic and tuff-rich volcani- clastic intercalations—ash-flow tuffs, ash-fall tuffs, lavas, tuffites—throughout the upper Lower to Upper Carbon- iferous succession. Top and bottom of the specimens were ground on a diamond lap to remove shape irregularities and magnetic contamination introduced during slicing. At least two duplicate specimens were prepared from each sample, allowing thermal demagnetisation of one specimen per sample. ate Triassic paleomagnetic studies are required for the Yangtze Block as well as for the NCB. Post-Late Triassic paleomagnetic poles have been computed for areas spread over the Yangtze Block [2,7^9]. The northwestern and southwestern parts of this block were subjected to Cenozoic intra-cratonic deformation [10^12], and paleo- magnetic poles from these areas can not be re- garded as representative of the stable block. It is therefore necessary to establish a characteristic paleomagnetic pole from a tectonically stable part of the Yangtze Block, in order to understand its relationship to the NCB. We have focused in this study on Late Jurassic formations from the Sichuan basin that is consid- ered to be a stable part of the Yangtze Block. Brief reviews and some geodynamic interpretation of the development of this region are given by Zubkov et al. (1989) and Ashchepkov et al. (1995). A ring of Mesozoic - Cenozoic alkaline-basalt volcanism has been found at the northern margin Minusinsk Depression. The volcanic pipes and dikes arc grouped over the margins of Kopievo dome-shaped uplift and located near flexures and main faults (Fig.1). These volcanic bodies represent the root system of volcanic eruptions, forming volcanic pipes of complex structure, lava necks and numerous dikes. Pipes mostly are multiphase structures composed of eruptive breccias with altered groundmass containing abundant debris of basalts and hypabyssal basanites. No cover facies have been identified. Despite textural variety of the basalts, their chemical composition remains constant, and they are all classed as basanites. The volcanic rocks have been intruded into Devonian- Carboniferous age terrigenous deposits. The K-Ar isotopic ages (Zubkov et al., 1989) for these four volcanic pipes are found within the range of 71-45 Ma. Two volcanoes (Bele and Tergeshskaya pipes), 545 546 V.Yu. Davidson a aSchool of Geology and Geophysics, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK 73119, USA bDepartment of Geology and Petroleum Geology, University of Aberdeen, King’s College, Aberdeen AB24 3UE Scotland, UK Abstract Paleomagnetic results suggest that there was a ﬂuid-ﬂow event which caused dolomitization and hematite authigenesis in serpentinite within the Highland Border Group along the Highland Boundary Fault in central Scotland in the late Carboniferous/ early Permian. Geochemical data indicate that the ﬂuid was hydrothermal in origin, and in addition to causing hematite authigenesis, the ﬂuid also thermally remagnetized pre-existing magnetite in the serpentinite. q 2000 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved. Keywords: remagnetization; ﬂuids; fault; paleomagnetism 1. Introduction In central Scotland, there are numerous exposures of red dolomite in the Caledonian (pre

HBF) in the Lower Paleozoic Highland Border Group (HBG). This study uses paleomagnetic analysis to date the ﬂuid migration event responsible for the dolomitiza- tion in the HBG and to assess whether the dolomite represents a single episode of ﬂuid-ﬂow and alteration of the basement, or if there were multiple events that are juxtaposed coincidentally. 2. Geological setting The trace of the HBF can be mapped with conﬁ- dence for a distance of 230 km from Stonehaven to Arran in central Scotland (Fig. 1). The predominant rocks to the north of the fault are Dalradian metasedi- ments whereas the rocks to the south are continental Devonian (Old Red Sandstone, ORS) sediments. At many places there is a narrow outcrop of the HBG, immediately south of the fault plane. These rocks represent an oceanic or backarc assemblage that has been excised almost completely. It includes several exposures of serpentinite, representing sea-ﬂoor basic rocks altered by meteoric ﬂuids (Ikin and Harmon, 1983). In some outcrops the serpentinite is massive. In others it is brecciated, either due to tectonic activity or synsedimentary processes. Outcrops of the serpentinite exhibit extensive dolo- mitization and/or siliciﬁcation. The alteration occurs partly as a massive replacement and partly as thin (from 1 to ,10 cm)

. Petrographic and geochemical studies are underway to assess this possibility. In summary, the results from the fault zone rocks in the HBF indicate that there was at least one dolomi- tizing and hematite-precipitating ﬂuid alteration event in central Scotland in the late Carboniferous. Measurement of the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility on the gabbroic samples reveals a flat-lying foliation with a radiating pattern of lineations, supporting the field evidence that the gabbros are part of a large, undeformed sill. Petrographic observations of oxides in the gabbros reveals two populations of magnetite grains produced during the original cooling of the sill: large, oxyexsolved titanomagnetite grains and fine-grained magnetite in igneous reaction rims. New 40Ar/39Ar age dating of biotite and plagioclase yield ages of V1.2 Ga, which represent the rapid cooling following emplacement of the mafic magma. A pilot collection (usually 25%–30% of the total number of samples) was randomly selected for each exposure. The pilot collection was subjected to detailed thermal demagnetization, and its results were used to choose an optimum regime of demagnetization, i.e., the temperature at which, supposedly, only the characteristic component remained in the sample. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. The following rejection criteria were employed: small signal values comparable with the instrumentation noise,

DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. The paleomagnetic poles from the study rocks clearly differ from younger poles of the Siberian Platform. All these data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component was acquired at the time of or shortly after the deposition of the Lakhandinskaya Group. Taking into account recent paleomagnetic data on the Middle Riphean Malginskaya Formation, results of this current work suggest, depending on the choice of the paleomagnetic direction polarity, two possible scenarios for relative movements of the Siberian Platform and Laurentia in a 1100–1000-Ma interval. One of these scenarios contradicts the hypothesis on Siberia as a part of the Rodinia supercontinent. The second scenario, which implies a variation in the generally accepted polarity for one of the cratonic blocks considered, is in a good agreement with this hypothesis but requires a coincidence of northern Laurentia with south-southeastern Siberia, rather than with its northern part, as is assumed in most reconstructions. A pilot collection (usually 25%–30% of the total number of samples) was randomly selected for each exposure. The pilot collection was subjected to detailed thermal demagnetization, and its results were used to choose an optimum regime of demagnetization, i.e., the temperature at which, supposedly, only the characteristic component remained in the sample. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. Thus, the available data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component formed during or soon after the deposition of the rocks studied. DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. The paleomagnetic poles from the study rocks clearly differ from younger poles of the Siberian Platform. All these data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component was acquired at the time of or shortly after the deposition of the Lakhandinskaya Group. Taking into account recent paleomagnetic data on the Middle Riphean Malginskaya Formation, results of this current work suggest, depending on the choice of the paleomagnetic direction polarity, two possible scenarios for relative movements of the Siberian Platform and Laurentia in a 1100–1000-Ma interval. One of these scenarios contradicts the hypothesis on Siberia as a part of the Rodinia supercontinent. The second scenario, which implies a variation in the generally accepted polarity for one of the cratonic blocks considered, is in a good agreement with this hypothesis but requires a coincidence of northern Laurentia with south-southeastern Siberia, rather than with its northern part, as is assumed in most reconstructions. A pilot collection (usually 25%–30% of the total number of samples) was randomly selected for each exposure. The pilot collection was subjected to detailed thermal demagnetization, and its results were used to choose an optimum regime of demagnetization, i.e., the temperature at which, supposedly, only the characteristic component remained in the sample. Spe- cial experiments designed to compare the results of thermal and alternating magnetic ﬁeld demagnetiza- tions showed a low efﬁciency of the latter. The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. The inferred results were used, upon rejection of a certain number of samples, for calculat- ing paleomagnetic directions and poles. The following rejection criteria were employed: small signal values comparable with the instrumentation noise,

The entire collection was then demagnetized using the chosen optimum regime. DISCUSSION The sequence of the individual paleomagnetic poles derived from the Lakhandinskaya rocks can provide detailed constraints on the movement of the Siberian craton in the earliest Late Riphean. However, within the framework of this work, mean paleomagnetic poles obtained for a relatively long time interval should apparently be used for solving the problem of the rela- tive position of Siberia and Laurentia. The paleomagnetic poles from the study rocks clearly differ from younger poles of the Siberian Platform. All these data point to the fact that the inferred characteristic component was acquired at the time of or shortly after the deposition of the Lakhandinskaya Group. Taking into account recent paleomagnetic data on the Middle Riphean Malginskaya Formation, results of this current work suggest, depending on the choice of the paleomagnetic direction polarity, two possible scenarios for relative movements of the Siberian Platform and Laurentia in a 1100–1000-Ma interval. One of these scenarios contradicts the hypothesis on Siberia as a part of the Rodinia supercontinent. The second scenario, which implies a variation in the generally accepted polarity for one of the cratonic blocks considered, is in a good agreement with this hypothesis but requires a coincidence of northern Laurentia with south-southeastern Siberia, rather than with its northern part, as is assumed in most reconstructions. Sampling We performed preliminary sampling on rocks span- ning a wide range of ages, locations, and structural orientations in northwestern Bulgaria (Fig. 1). Results reveal that the formations yielding the best results are of Triassic age, leading us to focus subsequent sampling on Upper Permian – Lower Triassic (‘‘Bundsandstein’’ red sandstone) and Middle – Upper Triassic (carbo- nates) units. In total, 8 sites (58 samples) in Lower Triassic, 19 sites (174 samples) in Middle – Upper Triassic, 1 site (14 samples) in Middle Jurassic, 4 sites (37 samples) in the Upper Jurassic, and 4 sites (34 samples) in the Lower Cretaceous rocks were obtained. The evolution of the deformation in this area was very different on either side of the present discontinuity. Thus, the deformation started along more or less parallel zones that possibly correspond to previous (sedimentary or tectonic) discontinuities. Around each ‘‘discontinuity’’, the overlying southern part acted as a rigid block, and the ‘‘folding’’ front advanced north- ward in the underlying northern part. Progressively, the whole unit was affected by the folding. 7. Conclusion The characteristic component of magnetization (ChRM A) observed in Upper Permian – Lower Tri- assic sediments in northwestern Bulgaria is likely a primary direction. The orientation of a secondary component (ChRM B) is believed to reflect a clock- wise rotation of this area relative to stable Europe after the beginning of the main Middle Eocene tectonic phase. The ChRM B provides a unique picture of the geological structures at an intermediate stage of defor- mation, and reveals that Eocene deformation began in the south and proceeded northwards. Brecciation The M-JC ore-bearing structures consist of two interrelated types of breccia bodies. ‘‘Breakthrough’’ structures cut one or more stratigraphic units. They are discordant bodies up to several thousand meters long, up to a few hundred meters wide, and up to >150 m high (Hoagland et al., 1965; Crawford et al., 1969). They may be V-shaped, low-domal or high- domal structures that appear to follow pre-mineralisa- tion faults and joints, and that are filled with a rubble breccia containing several petrographic types of clasts (McCormick et al., 1971; Hill, 1969; Hill et al., 1971a; Hoagland, 1976). Crackle breccias are found around the top and sides of the breakthrough struc- tures. The Immel, Young and New Market ore bodies are in ‘‘breakthrough’’ breccias. ‘‘Bedded’’ structures occur only within certain limestone beds in the King- sport Formation. They are semi-concordant tabular mantos of dolomitisation, brecciation and mineralisa- tion that appear to extend laterally from breakthrough breccia bodies in most cases (Kendall, 1960; Ful- weiler and McDougal, 1971). These bedded bodies rarely exceed more than tens of meters wide in length Fig. 3.

Brecciation The M-JC ore-bearing structures consist of two interrelated types of breccia bodies. ‘‘Breakthrough’’ structures cut one or more stratigraphic units. They are discordant bodies up to several thousand meters long, up to a few hundred meters wide, and up to >150 m high (Hoagland et al., 1965; Crawford et al., 1969). They may be V-shaped, low-domal or high- domal structures that appear to follow pre-mineralisa- tion faults and joints, and that are filled with a rubble breccia containing several petrographic types of clasts (McCormick et al., 1971; Hill, 1969; Hill et al., 1971a; Hoagland, 1976). Crackle breccias are found around the top and sides of the breakthrough struc- tures. The Immel, Young and New Market ore bodies are in ‘‘breakthrough’’ breccias. ‘‘Bedded’’ structures occur only within certain limestone beds in the King- sport Formation. They are semi-concordant tabular mantos of dolomitisation, brecciation and mineralisa- tion that appear to extend laterally from breakthrough breccia bodies in most cases (Kendall, 1960; Ful- weiler and McDougal, 1971). These bedded bodies rarely exceed more than tens of meters wide in length Fig. 3.

At first glance, the M- JC district seems to provide a poor fit to this correlation because the Acadian and Alleghanian orogenies are thought to span from f 390 to f 350 and from f 320 to f 250 Ma, respectively (Hatcher et al., 1989; Gar- ven et al., 1993), leaving the 316 F 8 Ma ore-forming event just straddling the start of the Alleghanian oro- geny. Introduction The Mascot – Jefferson City Mississippi V alley- type (MVT) zinc deposits are located in the V alley and Ridge physiographic province of the Appalachian orogen in eastern Tennessee (Fig. 1). They have been in fairly continuous production since 1854, and were the main source of zinc for the USA from the mid- 1950s to about 1990, providing more than half of its production at times (Fulweiler and Hill, 1992). Brecciation The M-JC ore-bearing structures consist of two interrelated types of breccia bodies. ‘‘Breakthrough’’ structures cut one or more stratigraphic units. They are discordant bodies up to several thousand meters long, up to a few hundred meters wide, and up to >150 m high (Hoagland et al., 1965; Crawford et al., 1969). They may be V-shaped, low-domal or high- domal structures that appear to follow pre-mineralisa- tion faults and joints, and that are filled with a rubble breccia containing several petrographic types of clasts (McCormick et al., 1971; Hill, 1969; Hill et al., 1971a; Hoagland, 1976). Crackle breccias are found around the top and sides of the breakthrough struc- tures. The Immel, Young and New Market ore bodies are in ‘‘breakthrough’’ breccias. ‘‘Bedded’’ structures occur only within certain limestone beds in the King- sport Formation. They are semi-concordant tabular mantos of dolomitisation, brecciation and mineralisa- tion that appear to extend laterally from breakthrough breccia bodies in most cases (Kendall, 1960; Ful- weiler and McDougal, 1971). At first glance, the M- JC district seems to provide a poor fit to this correlation because the Acadian and Alleghanian orogenies are thought to span from f 390 to f 350 and from f 320 to f 250 Ma, respectively (Hatcher et al., 1989; Gar- ven et al., 1993), leaving the 316 F 8 Ma ore-forming event just straddling the start of the Alleghanian oro- geny. This is awkward because the M-JC ore-forming event is shown to be post-folding yet appears to occur almost at the start of the Alleghanian orogeny. The time span of the Acadian orogeny in the central Appalachian orogen is fairly consistently defined. In their summary article, Osberg et al. (1989) gave a span from f 415 to f 360 Ma with peak orogenesis at f 390 Ma based broadly on radiometric, metamor- phic, structural, and other evidence. Garven et al. (1993) set the limits at f 395 and f 350 Ma for the purpose of hydrologic modeling. Hamilton-Smith (1993) leaned heavily on sedimentological evidence and placed the limits at f 390 and f 360 Ma. art of the Kisseynew Domain of the Trans-Hudson Orogen (THO) in north-central Manitoba. The dome is circular, about 6 km in diameter, with steeply-dipping flanks. It is composed of upper amphibolite-facies gneisses derived from turbiditic sediments, with leucogranitic sill-like intru - sions that were metamorphosed, starting at about 1830 Ma. Alternating field and thermal step demagnetization of 153 specimens from 17 sites around the perimeter of the dome isolated a characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) di - rection of D = 346.6°, I = 78.9° ( a 95 = 5.3°, k = 46, N = 17) that gives a pole of 119.5° W, 75.8° N ( dp = 9.5°, dm = 10.0°). Unblocking temperatures and saturation isothermal remanence analyses show that the ChRM resides mostly in single to pseudosingle domain magnetite or titanomagnetite, with minor hematite commonly present and with minor pyrrhotite present in the leucogranites. The ChRM is found to be postfolding with >>99.9% confidence, indicating ac - quisition on cooling from peak metamorphism at ~1810 ± 10 Ma. This Wapisu gneiss dome paleopole is the first from the Kisseynew Domain and the first from the 1830 to 1770 Ma interval in the THO. It indicates an ~90° bend or hair - pin in the apparent polar wander path for the THO juvenile terranes and Superior craton. It is speculated

At 72% unfolding, the Williston paleopole is rotated by 10 ± 12° clockwise with respect to the Early Cretaceous North America reference paleopole (124–88 Ma) of Van Fossen and Kent (1992; latitude 71.2°N, longitude 194.1°E), whereas at 100% unfolding the Williston paleopole is rotated by 19 ± 10° counterclockwise from this reference pole. At 87% unfolding, where directional grouping is best, the angular distance between the Williston and Cretaceous reference paleopoles is 7.5 ± 9°, whereas at 80% unfolding the paleopoles are also statistically indistin - guishable (Fig. 8). We suggest that Triassic rocks at Williston Lake were remagnetized during the initial stages of the Cretaceous– Cenozoic Laramide orogenic phase between 72 and 100% unfolding. The exclusive occurrence of normal polarity directions can then be reconciled with remanence acquisition during either the Cretaceous long normal superchron, a period of the Earth’s magnetic field from about 118 to 84 Ma characterized by stable normal polarity, or perhaps one of the somewhat shorter, but still appreciable in length, normal polarity chrons in the Late Cretaceous (e.g., C33n). L’objectif était de s’assurer de la pertinence de ces unités pour une étude magnéto-bio-stratigraphique détaillée visant à améliorer l’échelle référentielle de temps de la polarité géomagnétique au Trias. e.g., Ogg and Steiner 1991; Kent et al. 1995; Gallet et al. 1996, 1998; Muttoni et al. 1997). The most complete sequence of Late Triassic to earliest Jurassic magnetic polarity reversals comes from the Newark conti - nental rift basin succession of eastern North America (Kent et al. 1995), which led to the construction of the first reliable GPTS for 30 Ma of the Late Triassic (Kent and Olsen 1999). Triassic stage boundaries are, however, historically based on marine biostratigraphy, essentially from ammonoids and conodonts. We performed a paleomagnetic reconnaissance at three classic sections of Middle and Late Triassic marine fossiliferous limestones around Williston Lake in northeastern British Columbia. These sections have provided an integrated conodont–ammonoid biostratigraphic scale for the North America Triassic marine realm (Orchard and Tozer 1997). This study is aimed at testing the suitability of these sections for more detailed magnetostratigraphic study to correlate the marine biostratigraphic zonation to the nonmarine Newark reference GPTS. In Late Cretaceous times, greater India broke away from Madagascar with voluminous igneous activity accompanying the continental break-up. A geochemi- cal study of the Madagascan flood basalts suggests that the Marion hot spot was an important source of melts at the southern end of the island (Mahoney et a/., 1991; Storey et a/., 1997). This is also supported by a palaeogeographic reconstruction placing Mada- gascar in the near vicinity of the Marion hot spot around Late Cretaceous times (Storey et a/., 1995; Torsvik et a/., 1998). GEOLOGY OF NICARAGUA Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben (McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1

, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivision of the Coyol Group. To the west of the depression, in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain, the rocks are predominantly of sedimentary origin and are assumed to have been deposited on a Nicoya Complex type of basement (Parsons Corporation Report 1972). The sediments, tuffaceous shale, siltstone, greywacke, sandstone and lime- stone, range in age from Cretaceous to Miocene (Rivas, Brito, Masachapa and El Fraile formations) and are overlain by sediments of similar composition to the El Salto Formation and the pyroclastic deposits of the La Sierra Group (McBirney & Williams 1965; Parsons Corporation Report 1972). Seyfried et al. (1987) regard the Upper Cretaceous Rivas and the Eocene Brito formations as parts of a continuous succession. The Masachapa Formation is Oligocene in age (Auer 1942, unpublished paper; Zoppis Bracci & Del Guidice 1958) and the boundary between the Brito and Masachapa formations has been interpreted as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965). Also, the contact between the Masachapa Formation and the overlying Miocene El Fraile Formation is regarded as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965; Kuang 1971) and the El Fraile Formation interﬁngers with part of the volcanic Tamarindo Formation. - dominantly volcanic rocks from the Miocene Lower Coyol Group and from assumed Oligocene–Palaeocene rocks of the Matagalpa Group were sampled. As the tectonic control was often poor, our ambition has been to collect samples of rocks of similar age but geographically well-separated in order to detect later local tectonic movements. To the west of the Nicaraguan Depression we collected sedimentary and intrusive rocks of the Rivas Formation, sedi- mentary rocks of the Brito Formation and volcanic rocks of the Tamarindo Formation. The ages of these formations are Upper Cretaceous, Eocene and Miocene–Pliocene, respectively. MINERALOGICAL STUDIES Petrographic and X-ray diffraction studies (Nystro ¨m & Levi 1985; Elming 1985) have been carried out on specimens of andesite, basalt and sedimentary rocks from a number of sites. Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite, is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Alth

K–Ar AND 40 Ar / 39 Ar RADIOMETRIC AGE DETERMINATIONS In order to constrain the ages of magnetizations in this study, we have dated samples from selected palaeomagnetic sites by the K–Ar and 40Ar /39Ar methods. Previous Rb–Sr and K–Ar dating of whole-rock and mineral phases (Zoppis Bracci 1961; Barr & Escalante 1969; McBirney & Williams 1965) from both the Highland and the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain were of poor resolution and indicate that many of the units may have been emplaced over a long duration. Dating the same samples and ﬂows for which we have stable magnetic directions allows us to avoid assigning ‘incorrect’ or estimated ages to the magnetization. The K–Ar age determinations were made by R. M. Macintyre at the Scottish Universities Research and Reactor Centre (Table 1). One–four palaeomagnetic samples from each of the 11 sites 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16 and 17 were analysed, including andesite and basalt from the Lower Coyol and Matagalpa groups and a diabase dy

es 16 and 17) and three were chosen from other localities of the Matagalpa Group (sites 8, 12 and 14). Samples were crushed and sieved and small chips from the 100–250 mm fraction were chosen for dating. Samples of Bern4B biotite with an assumed age of 17.25t 0.20 Myr were used to monitor the neutron ﬂux. The samples were irradiated for 2 MW h in position 5c of the uranium-enriched research reactor of McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada. The samples were step-heated from about 500 to 1600 uC. The puriﬁed argon isotopes were then analysed in a Nuclide 6-60-SGA mass spectrometer at the Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska, Fairbanks, USA. Argon puriﬁcation was achieved using a liquid nitrogen cold trap SAES Zr–Al getter at 400 uC. The measured argon isotopes were corrected for system blank and mass discrimination as well as calcium, potassium and chlorine interference reactions following the procedures outlined in McDougall & Harrison (1988). Plateau ages were based on the criteria of three or more contiguous fractions accounting for more than 50 per cent gas release having ages within a 2s (95 per cent conﬁdence level) of the mean age. ical evidence, most of the samples dated by the 40Ar /39Ar method show either signiﬁcant argon loss or signiﬁcant argon gain. If these signs of alteration are prevalent throughout the sample suite, then interpretation of the K–Ar ages is difﬁcult. Nevertheless, we can infer that the age of the Tamarindo Group of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain is c. 15 Myr, samples correlative with the Lower Coyol Group are c. 18 Myr, the La Batea member of the Matagalpa Formation is c. 20 Myr, Matagalpa sites 8, 9 and 12 are c. 24 Myr and sites 13 and 14 are c. 30 Myr. section_candidates.excerpt: RAGUA Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben (McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation Report 1972), characterized by basaltic rocks overlain by inter- mediate to acid volcanic rocks. Ehrenborg (1996) has explained the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivis

Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite, is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Although the remanent magnetization of haematite is usually more resistant to demagnetization than magnetite, no signiﬁcant relation between degree of martitization and directional variations of the characteristic magnetizations was found. These rocks yield directions of magnetization (Fig. 6a) of reversed and dual polarities, signiﬁcantly different from those of the La Batea Formation. The declinations vary from c. 90u to 140uE and the inclinations are predominantly negative and lower than c. 30u. It is possible to distinguish two groups of directions with signiﬁcantly different declinations of c. 130uE (sites 8, 9 and 12) and 90uE (sites 13 and 14), respectively. The rocks of the two groups are sampled from geographically well-separated areas (Fig. 3). The coercivity of remanence of the ﬁrst group varies but the directions are fairly stable after being demagnetized in 10 mT AF. The rock at site 8 carries characteristic magnetizations of dual polarity, which may indicate that the rock at this site has not been remagnetized. As for the La Batea Formation the mean directions of the sites (Table 2) show that the inclinations are different while the declinations are quite similar. section_candidates.excerpt: RAGUA Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben (McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation Report 1972), characterized by basaltic rocks overlain by inter- mediate to acid volcanic rocks. Ehrenborg (1996) has explained the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivis

As the tectonic control was often poor, our ambition has been to collect samples of rocks of similar age but geographically well-separated in order to detect later local tectonic movements. To the west of the Nicaraguan Depression we collected sedimentary and intrusive rocks of the Rivas Formation, sedi- mentary rocks of the Brito Formation and volcanic rocks of the Tamarindo Formation. The ages of these formations are Upper Cretaceous, Eocene and Miocene–Pliocene, respectively. MINERALOGICAL STUDIES Petrographic and X-ray diffraction studies (Nystro ¨m & Levi 1985; Elming 1985) have been carried out on specimens of andesite, basalt and sedimentary rocks from a number of sites. Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite, is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Alth

ical evidence, most of the samples dated by the 40Ar /39Ar method show either signiﬁcant argon loss or signiﬁcant argon gain. If these signs of alteration are prevalent throughout the sample suite, then interpretation of the K–Ar ages is difﬁcult. Nevertheless, we can infer that the age of the Tamarindo Group of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain is c. 15 Myr, samples correlative with the Lower Coyol Group are c. 18 Myr, the La Batea member of the Matagalpa Formation is c. 20 Myr, Matagalpa sites 8, 9 and 12 are c. 24 Myr and sites 13 and 14 are c. 30 Myr. Age summary Based on our new geochronological evidence, most of the samples dated by the 40Ar /39Ar method show either signiﬁcant argon loss or signiﬁcant argon gain. The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). Ehrenborg (1996) has explained the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivision of the Coyol Group. The sediments, tuffaceous shale, siltstone, greywacke, sandstone and lime- stone, range in age from Cretaceous to Miocene (Rivas, Brito, Masachapa and El Fraile formations) and are overlain by sediments of similar composition to the El Salto Formation and the pyroclastic deposits of the La Sierra Group (McBirney & Williams 1965; Parsons Corporation Report 1972). Seyfried et al. (1987) regard the Upper Cretaceous Rivas and the Eocene Brito formations as parts of a continuous succession. The Masachapa Formation is Oligocene in age (Auer 1942, unpublished paper; Zoppis Bracci & Del Guidice 1958) and the boundary between the Brito and Masachapa formations has been interpreted as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965). Also, the contact between the Masachapa Formation and the overlying Miocene El Fraile Formation is regarded as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965; Kuang 1971) and the El Fraile Formation interﬁngers with part of the volcanic Tamarindo Formation. Also in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain secondary zeolite and clay minerals are found originating from alterations of volcaniclastics in the sedi- mentary units (Levi et al. 1990). The secondary minerals show a vertical zoning typical of burial diagenesis, which is a process controlled by an increase in temperature with depth. A palaeo- thermal gradient of about 15–20 uCk m x1 is estimated for the Cretaceous to Oligocene diagenetic episodes and the temper- ature in the lower parts of the Rivas, Brito and Masachapa formations is estimated at c. 120 uC. Mineralogical breaks are observed between the Masachapa and Brito formations as well as between the Brito and Rivas formations . These breaks were suggested to reﬂect tectonic events of regional character (Levi et al. 1990), possibly related to changes in the polarity of subduction. This study shows the existence of three magnetization components. Two of them are interpreted as Cenozoic and Permian remagnetizations; their poles are 88.8 uN, 164.0 uE, K=262, A 95=3.3u and 43.4 uS, 61.7uE, K=93, A95=5.9u, respectively. Its corresponding palaeomagnetic pole (28.3 uS, 58.9uE, K=157, A 95=4.2u) is close to the poles from the Saharan platform obtained from neighbouring periods. The positive fold test of this study thus validates these previous Upper Palaeozoic poles. This new result is in agreement with the geodynamical model (Matte 1986; Henryet al. 1992), which proposed the occurrence of a large clockwise rotation of Africa during the Carboniferous; such a motion agrees with the Permian Pangaea A2 reconstruction. INTRODUCTION In order to improve the African palaeomagnetic database for Palaeozoic times, which is still poor, we have undertaken, during the last 10 years, systematic palaeomagnetic studies of the dated tabular formations of the Illizi basin (SE Algeria, Fig. 1a). Levels of various ages, ranging from the Silurian to the Albian, were analysed. These studies led to the determination of ﬁve new African palaeomagnetic poles. The ﬁrst, determined in the ‘El Adeb Larache’ area, is of Moscovian age (Henryet al. 1992), the second is of Stephano–Autunian age from the Tiguentourine For

, the third is from the Middle Zarzaı¨tine Formation of Liassic–Dogger age (Derder et al . 1994b), the fourth, determined in the ‘la Recule´e’ area from the Lower Zarzaitine is of Triassic–Liassic age (Kieset al. 1995), and the ﬁfth is of Bashkirian age from the Oubarakat Formation (Derder et al. 2001a). These studies also showed the existence of Cenozoic and Permian remagnetization events. However, as in most of the palaeomagnetic studies in hori- zontal tabular areas, the age of the magnetization acquisition has not been demonstrated. Indeed, in all cases, geological and geophysical constraints did not permit palaeomagnetic tests, except a reversal test in the Lower Zarzaı ¨tine Formation of Triassic–Liassic age (Kies et al. 1995). Such a reversal test is not absolute proof of the primary character of the magnetization, but indicates that the magnetization consists of a single com- ponent. The only argument in favour of the primary character of the magnetization is the variation of its direction from one formation to another, while the magnetic overprints (Permian and Cenozoic) observed at some levels have the same orientation in the different geological formations. To validate the previous results by a fold test, a new study was carried out 60 km SE of In Amenas city, in the Edjeleh region

During demagnetization, after eventual elimination of a small viscous component, the analysis of the magnetization directions of the samples gives two different kinds of results: a stable magnetic direction characteristic of an apparently single component, or directions evolving along a great circle, which shows the superimposition of unblocking temperature spectra for at least two components. INTRODUCTION In order to improve the African palaeomagnetic database for Palaeozoic times, which is still poor, we have undertaken, during the last 10 years, systematic palaeomagnetic studies of the dated tabular formations of the Illizi basin (SE Algeria, Fig. 1a). Levels of various ages, ranging from the Silurian to the Albian, were analysed. These studies led to the determination of ﬁve new African palaeomagnetic poles. The ﬁrst, determined in the ‘El Adeb Larache’ area, is of Moscovian age (Henryet al. 1992), the second is of Stephano–Autunian age from the Tiguentourine For

, the third is from the Middle Zarzaı¨tine Formation of Liassic–Dogger age (Derder et al . 1994b), the fourth, determined in the ‘la Recule´e’ area from the Lower Zarzaitine is of Triassic–Liassic age (Kieset al. 1995), and the ﬁfth is of Bashkirian age from the Oubarakat Formation (Derder et al. 2001a). These studies also showed the existence of Cenozoic and Permian remagnetization events. However, as in most of the palaeomagnetic studies in hori- zontal tabular areas, the age of the magnetization acquisition has not been demonstrated. Indeed, in all cases, geological and geophysical constraints did not permit palaeomagnetic tests, except a reversal test in the Lower Zarzaı ¨tine Formation of Triassic–Liassic age (Kies et al. 1995). Such a reversal test is not absolute proof of the primary character of the magnetization, but indicates that the magnetization consists of a single com- ponent. The only argument in favour of the primary character of the magnetization is the variation of its direction from one formation to another, while the magnetic overprints (Permian and Cenozoic) observed at some levels have the same orientation in the different geological formations. The Sierras Australes fold and thrust belt of Buenos Aires province (Argentina) has been interpreted as being the result of a crustal collision between these two blocks. A palaeomagnetic study of the less deformed upper part of the Permian Tunas Formation of the Pillahuinco ´ region within the Sierras Australes belt was carried out in order to obtain reliable palaeomagnetic poles to constrain the palaeogeographic and tectonic evolution of this part of Gondwana. More than 300 specimens were measured from the Tunas Formation in the Sierra de Pillahuinco´ , from 27 sites in four localities of these red sandstones and clay-siltstones. Palaeogeographically, these two Tunas Formation poles are interpreted as recording a slight counterclockwise movement of South America during the Permian. Key words: Gondwana, palaeomagnetism, Palaeozoic, Sierras Australes, South America, tectonics. INTRODUCTION The southwestern margin of Gondwanaland was located north of the Colorado River during the Palaeozoic, and marks the boundary between the South America craton to the north and the Patagonia region to the south (Fig. 1). The Sierras Australes orogenic belt trends approximately NW–SE in the southwestern part of Buenos Aires province (Figs 1 and 2), and is considered to be the South American counterpart of the Cape Fold Belt in South Africa (Du Toit 1927). Its geological features have attracted the attention of many geologists since the early 1900s because it is a key to understanding the controversial evolution of this part of Gondwana. For some authors, the Sierras Australes are the result of intracontinental deformation exclusively (Selle´s Martı´nez 1989; Cobbold et al. 1991; Japas 1989); for others, the Sierras Australes are the result of the collision of the Patagonia terrane with Gondwana (Dalmayrac et al . 1980; Ramos 1984; Tomezzoli 1997). The deforma

alaeomagnetic study was to obtain additional reliable palaeomagnetic poles to evaluate the palaeogeographic and geo- dynamic evolution of this area, and therefore of Gondwana, building on the earlier study of Tomezzoli & Vilas (1999). Most of them were quite stable during the early heating steps and started to demagnetize between 500 and 680 uC with a gradual quasi-linear decay towards the origin (Figs 3a and b). Other samples displayed an abrupt decay of a very stable remanence (Fig. 3c). Unblocking temperatures between 630 and 680 uC clearly show that this magnetization is carried by haematite. In some samples from Las Mostazas, the demagnetization paths were curved, along great circles towards the southeast quadrant with positive inclination, indicating simultaneous removal of distinct mag- netic components with overlapping unblocking temperatures (Fig. 3d). Assuming this, the method of McFadden & McElhinny (1988) was used to analyse these cases. Unblocking temper- atures of samples from the Las Mostazas locality range between 450 and 680 uC, showing that this magnetization is carried by magnetite, haematite or both. Further rock-magnetic studies are required to conﬁrm the magneto-mineralogy. Some investigators have suggested that there may have been more than one tectonic phase in this area, and postulated an early deformation phase of Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous age that preceded the widely recognized Upper Palaeozoic phase (Kilmurray 1975; Varela 1978; Ramos 1984, 1988; Tomezzoli 1997). Tomezzoli & Vilas (1999) reported the presence of a syn- tectonic magnetization carried by haematite (at 42 per cent unfolding) in the red sandstone and clay siltstone of the lower part of the Tunas Formation in the Sierra de las Tunas region (Fig. 2). They concluded that the lower part of the Tunas Formation was deformed and remagnetized very soon after its deposition in the Early Permian. According to Ramos (1984), along the northern boundary of Patagonia and southern margin of Gondwana, an ocean was consumed by subduction beneath Patagonia, the subduction ceasing with the collision of the continental blocks. na associations of the Tunas Formation indicate an Early Permian to early Late Permian age for these rocks (Harrington 1947; Archangelsky & Cu´ neo 1984). PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS We sampled oriented blocks, from which we cut from two to ﬁve oriented 8 cm 3 cubic samples. A total of 400 samples from different hand blocks were studied from 58 sites and 17 localities. Except for some Palaeozoic traps of the Viluy and Markha rivers, all directions were calculated using only in situ coordinates in the absence of any folding on the Siberian platform. Stepwise thermal demagnetizations and magnetic measure- ments of the samples were carried out in the Irkutsk palaeo- magnetic laboratory (80 per cent of the samples) and in the palaeomagnetic laboratory of the Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris (IPGP; 20 per cent of the samples). Tables in this paper include two statistical levels: site averages based on samples and locality averages based on sites. Thermal demagnetization was performed in Irkutsk using ovens housed in three concentric m-metal shields. The residual ﬁeld is about 10 nT in the centre of the ovens. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics.
